name: Zonisamide (Zonegran, Zonisade)
summary: Long-acting antiseizure medication sometimes used off-label in psychiatry for binge eating disorder, especially when appetite, cravings, and weight are part of the picture. Can help some people, but it’s not a first-line psych med and it comes with real safety monitoring (metabolic acidosis, kidney stones, mood changes).
description: Zonisamide is an antiseizure medication that also has off-label psychiatric use for binge eating disorder. Some people notice reduced appetite and fewer binge urges over weeks. Common side effects include sleepiness, dizziness, appetite loss, and “brain slowing.” Serious risks include metabolic acidosis, kidney stones, severe rashes (SJS/TEN), and psychiatric effects like depression or psychosis. It should be tapered down gradually if you’ve been on it long-term.
patient_summary: Zonisamide is sometimes used off-label for binge eating disorder when the goal is fewer binge urges and less appetite-driven eating. It’s long-acting, so changes are usually gradual. The tradeoff: it can cause fatigue, dizziness, appetite loss, and cognitive slowing, and it requires safety monitoring (especially bicarbonate and kidney function). Tell your clinician right away if you notice depression, suicidal thoughts, confusion, or new paranoia/hallucinations.

linked_conditions.context: Used off-label in some adults with binge eating disorder, especially when appetite, cravings, and weight are clinically relevant. Not considered a first-line option; careful monitoring is required due to metabolic, renal, dermatologic, and psychiatric risks.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to zonisamide, sulfonamides, or any component of the formulation

efficacy_response.patient_text: For binge eating disorder, zonisamide has off-label study support, but response varies a lot. If it helps, people typically notice fewer binge urges and reduced appetite over weeks—not overnight. Because it can also cause cognitive slowing and mood changes, the goal is “benefit without wrecking your day.”

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Rapid (food may delay time to peak but does not meaningfully change absorption)
pharmacokinetics.onset: Not immediate; psychiatric effects (appetite/craving changes) are typically gradual over days to weeks
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Long-acting due to long half-life (often dosed once daily, sometimes divided)
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic (CYP3A4); also acetylation and reduction pathways
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine (including a portion as unchanged drug)
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food delays time to peak; can be taken with or without food

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: In psychiatry, zonisamide is mainly an off-label option for {link:condition:binge-eating-disorder:binge eating disorder}—usually when appetite, cravings, and weight are part of the clinical picture and more standard treatments aren’t a great fit or haven’t helped enough. This is not a first-line binge eating medication, and it requires real monitoring.
items: {link:condition:binge-eating-disorder:Binge Eating Disorder (off-label)}: May reduce appetite and binge urges in some adults over time
Cravings-driven eating patterns: Sometimes considered when overeating is strongly appetite-driven (off-label, clinician-dependent)
Weight-related considerations: Some people lose weight on it, which can be a goal for some patients and a problem for others

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Zonisamide can feel “quiet” in the background—until it doesn’t. Here’s how people commonly describe it:

quotes: It didn’t flip a switch, but my cravings got less loud over a couple weeks.
I noticed I could pause before a binge instead of feeling pulled by a magnet.
Food felt less urgent. Not gone—just less bossy.
I felt kind of wiped out at first—like my battery was stuck on low.
Sleepiness was real, especially when the dose went up.
I wasn’t depressed, but I felt slowed down.
items.note: Fatigue and drowsiness are common, especially during titration or at higher doses.

quotes: My brain felt a little laggy—like a slow Wi-Fi connection.
I struggled with word-finding and staying sharp at work.
It helped my eating, but I hated the mental fog.
items.note: Psychomotor slowing and concentration issues can show up early and are more common at higher doses.

quotes: My mood dipped in a way that didn’t feel like ‘normal stress.’
I got more irritable and edgy for no clear reason.
I felt mentally off—like my thoughts weren’t lining up right.
items.note: Zonisamide can worsen depression or trigger unusual psychiatric symptoms (including psychosis) in a small subset of people. This is a stop-and-call-your-clinician situation.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Zonisamide is long-acting. For binge eating, it’s not a “take it and feel it” medication—benefits are usually gradual, and side effects can appear early during titration.
key_points: Hours: Blood levels rise and peak after a dose (timing depends on formulation and food)
Days to weeks: Appetite and binge-urge changes (if they happen) are typically gradual
Long half-life (~63 hours): It builds up slowly and washes out slowly
Once-daily dosing often works: Some people do better with divided dosing if side effects spike

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: For binge eating disorder, zonisamide can help some people with appetite and binge urges, but it’s not a guaranteed win and it’s not first-line. The practical reality: if it helps, you’ll usually notice fewer urges and less “drive” to binge over a few weeks. If it doesn’t help—or if side effects are loud (fatigue, brain fog, mood drop)—the cost can outweigh the benefit.
sections.clinical_details: Because BED use is off-label, dosing and expectations are more individualized than with FDA-approved BED medications. Clinicians typically use slow titration and keep a close eye on mood symptoms, cognition, bicarbonate (metabolic acidosis risk), and kidney stone risk.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Call your clinician urgently for new depression, suicidal thoughts, confusion, paranoia, hallucinations, severe rash, vision pain, or signs of metabolic acidosis.
other: Severe skin reactions can occur early (Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis). Stop and get urgent evaluation for rash with fever, mucosal sores, blistering, or peeling skin.
Psychiatric and cognitive effects: Can cause depression, agitation, psychosis, slowed thinking, speech/language issues, and fatigue—often within the first month and more commonly at higher doses.

Metabolic acidosis: Can occur even at low doses. Risk is higher with kidney disease, severe lung disease, diarrhea, ketogenic diet, status epilepticus, or certain other meds. Monitoring bicarbonate matters.
Kidney stones (nephrolithiasis) and kidney function changes: Can raise BUN/creatinine and increase stone risk.
Eye emergency risk: Acute myopia and secondary angle-closure glaucoma can happen, often within the first month. Sudden blurry vision and/or eye pain = urgent care.
Suicidal thoughts/behavior: Antiseizure medications as a class carry an increased risk. Monitor closely, especially early on or after dose changes.
Sulfonamide (“sulfa”) allergy: Labeling lists sulfonamide hypersensitivity as a contraindication. Cross-reactivity risk is debated, but severe past reactions (like SJS/TEN) are a big red flag.
patient_counseling: Don’t ignore mood changes. If you feel darker, more hopeless, or have suicidal thoughts, reach out immediately.
Hydration matters. Kidney stones are a known risk—drink fluids unless your clinician told you otherwise.
If you get a rash—especially with fever, mouth sores, or blistering—stop the medication and get urgent evaluation.
If you develop sudden blurry vision or eye pain, treat it like an emergency.
Heat intolerance and reduced sweating can happen (more common in kids). If you’re overheating or not sweating normally, take it seriously.
Tell your clinician about kidney disease, lung disease, a ketogenic diet, or other meds like topiramate or valproate before starting.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: sleepiness, dizziness, appetite loss, nausea, and cognitive slowing. Psychiatric effects (depression, agitation, psychosis) are less common but clinically serious.
plain_language_list: Reduced appetite and weight loss (can be desired or problematic)
Insomnia (yes, some people get sleepy and still sleep worse)
Kidney stones (less common, but a known risk)

common.patient_note: This can hit early, especially during dose increases. If you feel unsafe to drive or function, that’s not something to “push through.” Dose timing or slower titration may help.
Often worse at initiation or when the dose jumps too fast. Standing up slowly and staying hydrated can help, but persistent dizziness should be discussed.
This is part of why it’s used off-label for BED, but it can also backfire (low energy, feeling unwell, triggering restrictive patterns). The goal is steady improvement, not feeling sick.

common.incidence: Common in clinical use; more likely at higher doses
common.patient_note: People describe brain fog, word-finding issues, and slower thinking. If your work/school performance takes a hit, that’s a real side effect—not a character flaw.
Taking it consistently with or without food (pick one and stick with it) can reduce surprises. Persistent GI issues deserve a dose or formulation discussion.

serious: Severe rash (SJS/TEN): fever, blistering, mucosal sores, peeling skin. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms): rash with fever, swollen lymph nodes, facial swelling, and organ involvement. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Metabolic acidosis: deep/rapid breathing, unusual fatigue, confusion, heart rhythm issues, bone effects over time. Requires lab monitoring and clinical action.
Psychiatric effects: new or worsening depression, suicidal thoughts, agitation, psychosis, severe confusion.
Acute myopia/angle-closure glaucoma: sudden vision changes and eye pain. URGENT EVALUATION.
Kidney stones or renal complications: flank pain, blood in urine, severe urinary symptoms.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Zonisamide has meaningful interactions through CYP3A4 (and to a lesser degree CYP2C19). Some combinations raise toxicity risk (metabolic acidosis, hyperammonemia, sedation, cognitive effects).

items.with: CYP3A4 Inducers (example: carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital; also some herbal products like St. John’s Wort)
items.risk: May lower zonisamide levels and reduce effectiveness. Dose needs can change, and abrupt changes can destabilize symptoms.
items.action: If combined, clinicians often adjust titration and monitor response more closely. Don’t add or stop inducers without medical guidance.

items.with: CYP3A4 Inhibitors (some macrolide antibiotics, azole antifungals, certain antivirals)
items.risk: May increase zonisamide exposure and side effects (sleepiness, brain fog, toxicity).
items.action: Monitor for side effects; clinicians may slow titration or adjust dose depending on the inhibitor and clinical response.

items.risk: Hyperammonemia and encephalopathy risk may increase when combined (especially if symptoms like lethargy, vomiting, or mental status changes occur).
items.action: If symptoms suggest encephalopathy, clinicians may check ammonia and adjust therapy promptly.

items.with: Topiramate or other carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
items.risk: Higher risk of metabolic acidosis and kidney stones, plus additive cognitive side effects.
items.action: Use caution; monitor bicarbonate and renal risks more closely. Hydration and symptom tracking matter.

items.risk: Ketogenic diets can increase acidosis risk; zonisamide can add to that risk.
items.action: Requires clinician oversight and more frequent bicarbonate monitoring if used together.

items.with: Alcohol or other sedating meds (sleep aids, sedating antihistamines, cannabis in some people)
items.risk: Additive sedation and impairment; can worsen cognitive slowing and coordination issues.
items.action: Be cautious, especially during titration. If you feel impaired, don’t drive or do risky tasks.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If you’ve been on zonisamide long-term, don’t stop suddenly. Even when it’s being used for psychiatric reasons, your nervous system can still react to abrupt withdrawal. Tapering is typically slow and individualized.
key_points: Why taper: Abrupt stopping can cause withdrawal-type symptoms (dysphoria, hallucinations, headache, insomnia, tremor) and—if the person has epilepsy—can increase seizure risk.

Typical pace (general guidance): Slow reductions over weeks to months are common for chronic therapy. Some clinicians taper antiseizure medications over a few to several months (for example, 2 to 6 months), depending on dose, duration, and patient stability.
Go slower if: Higher doses, longer duration, significant side effects during past dose changes, or if mood destabilizes during taper.
If serious safety issues happen (severe rash, suspected DRESS, eye emergency, severe psychiatric reaction): Discontinuation may need to be faster under medical supervision.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: For binge eating disorder, zonisamide dosing is off-label and varies by clinician and patient factors. The main theme is slow titration and watching for cognitive and mood side effects.

adult.bed_initial: Option A (commonly used in studies): 100 mg PO daily for 7 days
adult.bed_titration: Increase by 100 mg/day each week based on response and tolerability
adult.bed_max: 600 mg/day PO in 1 or 2 divided doses (higher doses often mean more side effects; many people won’t tolerate going that high)
adult.bed_lower_dose_alternative: Option B (lower-dose strategy studied): 25 mg PO daily for 7 days; increase by 50 mg/day each week based on response and tolerability
adult.bed_bmi_based_max: With the lower-dose strategy: max 100 mg/day if BMI <35 kg/m²; max 150 mg/day if BMI ≥35 kg/m²

sections.simple_explanation: This is a slow-build medication with a long half-life. If you jump doses too fast, side effects like fatigue and brain fog can show up hard. The goal is the lowest dose that helps binge urges without making you feel dulled, depressed, or cognitively slowed.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Zonisamide requires extra caution in pregnancy, breastfeeding, kidney disease, and older adults. For psychiatric use, the risk/benefit conversation matters even more because there are often alternative options.
sections.pregnancy: Zonisamide crosses the placenta. Data are insufficient to clearly define risk of specific major birth defects and neurodevelopmental outcomes, so pregnancy use is a careful shared decision. Pregnancy can increase clearance and lower blood levels as pregnancy progresses, which may change effectiveness. Newborns exposed in utero should be monitored for transient metabolic acidosis. If used during pregnancy, clinicians may monitor trough levels and adjust doses to maintain stability, with a plan to return to pre-pregnancy dosing after delivery. People who can become pregnant should use effective contraception during therapy and for 1 month after the last dose.
sections.lactation: Zonisamide is present in breast milk, and reported relative infant doses can be high. Some case reports describe no observed adverse events, but infant serum levels can be substantial. Manufacturer guidance is to weigh infant exposure risk, breastfeeding benefits, and treatment benefits to the mother. If breastfeeding while on zonisamide, infants should be monitored for sedation, feeding issues, weight gain, lab abnormalities (platelets, liver function), developmental milestones, and heat intolerance/reduced sweating.
sections.geriatrics: Refer to adult dosing, but start at the low end and titrate slowly. Older adults may be more sensitive to sedation, dizziness, cognitive slowing, and fall risk. Monitor kidney function and bicarbonate closely, and reassess whether the benefit is worth the burden.
sections.hepatic: No formal dose adjustments are provided in labeling, but slower titration and frequent monitoring are recommended in hepatic impairment. Use with caution.
sections.renal: Manufacturer recommends avoiding use when eGFR <50 mL/min due to limited dosing/toxicity experience. For eGFR ≥30 mL/min, no initial adjustment is generally needed. For eGFR <30 mL/min, consider alternatives or use with caution using slow titration and frequent monitoring; therapeutic drug monitoring (when available) can help. Dialysis and CRRT settings may remove drug; dosing and monitoring may need individualized adjustment.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Mood and safety: Screen for depression, suicidality, agitation, behavioral changes—especially in the first weeks and after dose increases.
Cognition and functioning: Watch for psychomotor slowing, concentration problems, speech/language issues, and overall day-to-day performance.
Serum bicarbonate: Check prior to initiation and periodically during therapy to monitor for metabolic acidosis.
Renal function: Periodic BUN and serum creatinine; assess kidney stone risk and hydration status.
Kidney stones (nephrolithiasis): Monitor for flank pain, hematuria, urinary symptoms; counsel on hydration.
Ammonia level: Check if symptoms suggest encephalopathy (unexplained lethargy, vomiting, confusion), especially with valproate or similar risk factors.
Heat intolerance/reduced sweating: Monitor for decreased sweating and elevated body temperature, especially in warm weather and in pediatric exposure scenarios.
Therapeutic drug monitoring (when available): Consider trough levels to optimize dosing or evaluate toxicity, especially in renal impairment, dialysis/CRRT, or pregnancy.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Zonisamide is taken orally as capsules or an oral suspension. Choose the form that makes adherence realistic (and accurate dosing possible).
items: Administration notes: Capsules should be swallowed whole. Suspension should be shaken well and measured with an oral syringe (not a kitchen spoon). Can be taken with or without food.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Zonisamide stabilizes overactive neurons by acting on sodium and calcium channels, which helps reduce abnormal firing patterns. It does not work by boosting GABA the way benzodiazepines do. In binge eating disorder, the benefit is thought to relate to downstream effects on appetite and reward-driven eating—not a direct ‘anti-anxiety’ mechanism.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: For binge eating disorder, zonisamide is a niche, off-label option—not a default. It may be considered when standard treatments haven’t helped enough, aren’t tolerated, or aren’t appropriate, and when appetite/weight effects are clinically relevant. The big clinical tension is this: it might reduce binge urges, but it can also cause fatigue, cognitive slowing, and mood problems. If you’re trading binge eating for brain fog and depression, that’s not a win.

seo.title: Zonisamide (Zonegran, Zonisade) for Binge Eating: Uses, Dosing, Side Effects & Safety
seo.description: Zonisamide (Zonegran/Zonisade) is an antiseizure medication sometimes used off-label for binge eating disorder. Learn dosing approaches, what people feel, side effects (fatigue, brain fog), and serious risks like metabolic acidosis, kidney stones, and mood changes.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.q: What is zonisamide used for in psychiatry?
faqs.a: In psychiatry, zonisamide is most often discussed as an off-label option for binge eating disorder. The goal is usually reduced appetite and fewer binge urges over time. It’s not a first-line BED treatment and it requires monitoring because it can affect mood, cognition, bicarbonate (metabolic acidosis), and kidney stone risk.

faqs.q: How long does zonisamide take to work for binge eating?
faqs.a: Usually not right away. Zonisamide has a long half-life and is titrated slowly. If it helps with binge urges or appetite, people often notice changes over days to weeks, not within hours.

It can. Appetite loss and weight loss are known effects for some people, which is part of why it’s considered off-label in binge eating disorder. But weight loss isn’t guaranteed, and for some people the side effects (fatigue, nausea, brain fog) are the bigger story.

faqs.q: Can zonisamide make depression or anxiety worse?
faqs.a: Yes, it can. Psychiatric side effects are a known risk: depression, irritability, agitation, anxiety, and—in rarer cases—psychosis. If you notice a mood drop, suicidal thoughts, paranoia, hallucinations, or feeling mentally “off,” contact your clinician immediately.

faqs.q: What labs should be monitored on zonisamide?
faqs.a: The big one is serum bicarbonate (to watch for metabolic acidosis), plus periodic kidney monitoring (BUN/creatinine). Clinicians may also check ammonia if encephalopathy symptoms occur (especially with valproate), and sometimes use trough drug levels in complex situations (renal impairment, pregnancy, dialysis/CRRT, or suspected toxicity).

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: Common side effects include drowsiness/fatigue, dizziness, decreased appetite, nausea, and cognitive slowing (brain fog, concentration issues, word-finding problems). Insomnia can also happen in some people.

faqs.q: What are the serious risks I should watch for?
faqs.a: Red-flag issues include severe rash (SJS/TEN), DRESS, metabolic acidosis, kidney stones, sudden vision changes/eye pain (possible angle-closure glaucoma), and serious psychiatric changes (suicidal thoughts, psychosis, severe confusion). Those require urgent medical attention.

faqs.q: Can I take zonisamide if I have kidney problems?
faqs.a: It depends. The manufacturer recommends avoiding use when eGFR is below 50 mL/min due to limited dosing/toxicity experience. Some clinical guidance suggests no initial adjustment is needed above certain thresholds, but slower titration and close monitoring are important in impaired kidney function—especially because of metabolic acidosis and kidney stone risk. This is a clinician-supervised decision.

faqs.q: Is zonisamide safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Pregnancy and breastfeeding require a careful risk/benefit discussion. Zonisamide crosses the placenta, and data are limited on specific malformation and neurodevelopment risks. In breastfeeding, zonisamide can pass into milk at relatively high levels in some reports, and infant serum levels can be significant. If used, clinicians typically emphasize monitoring and individualized planning.

faqs.q: Do I need to taper zonisamide to stop it?
faqs.a: If you’ve been on it long-term, yes—tapering is typically recommended. Stopping abruptly can cause withdrawal-type symptoms (like insomnia, tremor, dysphoria, even hallucinations) and can be dangerous for people with seizure risk. Your prescriber will build a step-down plan that fits your dose, duration, and symptoms.
